state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think about it this way: if you were moving a bookshelf in your room, would you push it up 3 units or would you move it in a different direction? Try connecting the abstract translation to a real-world scenario that you can visualize.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so you'd push it sideways, not up... but I'm still confused about which way though? Like, is it to the right or left? And how does that connect to the minus 3 in the brackets?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were rearranging your furniture in your room — would you move the bookshelf to the right or to the left by 3 units? Think about how this real-world scenario connects to the minus 3 in the brackets of the function.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses a vague real-world analogy that doesn't address the specific misconception about why x-3 moves right (not up), and the student remains confused about the direction and connection to the algebraic form by the end.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses a concrete real-world analogy (moving a bookshelf in a room) to help the student visualize and understand the abstract concept of function transformation, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
